plan.strategy: Establish the measured baseline for the injected best-so-far seed (aligned-address direct launcher, dtype-capped UB block, stride-correct in-place writes).
plan.code_changes: None; seed written verbatim to tmp/main.py.
plan.hypothesis: The seed is correct on all 36 workloads and gives the starting latency for the 12 timing cases.

profile.summary: mixed: Small cases are host/launch-bound: the device task is 12.6% of the evaluated walltime, At identical element count and identical logical bytes, the non-fp16 fp32-math path costs 2.08x the fp16 vector time, Scalar prologue cost is purely per-program; the 8192 block cap doubles it on bf16/fp32 without evidence of internal sub-tiling

conclusion.root_cause: Baseline established: 36/36 PASS, geo_mean 0.825. Two independent bottlenecks identified. (1) Nine of the twelve timing workloads are host-launch bound: profiled device task duration for selu_-timing-0 (fp16 [1024]) is 1.65 us against a 13.16 us walltime, and a target-side host-cost probe measured the candidate's per-call host path at 12.17 us versus 11.5 us for the PyTorch reference wrapper shape and 9.2 us for the bare compiled-launcher floor. (2) The three large workloads are device bound and dominated by the number of MTE transfers rather than by bytes or program count: the candidate runs fp16 [4096,4096] at 45.6 us (vector 27.2 us), bf16 at 83.2 us (vector 56.7 us) and fp32 at 82.6 us (vector 46.3 us); a target probe shows a pure copy kernel at BLOCK 16384 costs 40.2 us versus 78.1 us at BLOCK 8192 for the same bytes, and 2 tiles per program at BLOCK 8192 costs 77.3 us, so device time tracks transfer count, and the fp32-domain math needs three full-width UB tiles live, which caps BLOCK at 8192 for bf16/fp32 (every BLOCK 16384 variant fails to compile with ub overflow, including enable_ubuf_saving and a tightened fma form).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: No previous measurement to compare against; this round fixes the reference point. Gap decomposition for the next experiments: on the nine host-bound workloads the candidate is 5.8% above its own achievable host floor (12.17 us measured vs 11.50 us for a prebound-method, numel-keyed, single-frame launch path) and 1.4x above the reference (10.47 us at timing-0); on the large workloads the transfer-count model predicts bf16 can move from 83.8 us to about 64.5 us if the fp32-domain math is replaced by fp16-width math so that BLOCK can double to 16384 (probed: 64.45 us, max abs error 0.0175 with 0 of 16777216 elements outside the bf16 tolerance), while fp32 has no compilable BLOCK 16384 form and stays transfer-bound.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Target the host-bound majority first: replace the per-call dispatch with the probed faster launch path (bound Tensor methods hoisted to module scope, dictionary keyed by numel instead of a (numel, align) tuple, launcher closures taking only the pointer, all inside a single Python frame) while still reading this call's address, dtype, contiguity and current stream, which the target probe measured at 11.50 us versus 12.17 us for the current path.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The three tensor-metadata reads, the dict key and the address-subclass construction each cost ~0.25-0.35 us in isolation but ~2.2 us in total under a saturated launch queue, so per-call Python work has to be judged under real queue pressure, not in a microbenchmark; and UB overflow is a compile-time error, so tile-width feasibility for each dtype can be enumerated cheaply before any measurement.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 is the injected best-so-far seed measured unchanged; profile plus target-side probes replaced guessing about which of the two regimes (host launch vs device transfer count) to attack, and they show the two require different changes, so the loop proceeds host-path first and tile/math-width second.

plan.strategy: Shrink the per-call host launch path while keeping this call's address, dtype, contiguity and current stream reads intact.
plan.code_changes: run() now reads only this call's address, numel, dtype, contiguity and (inside the launcher) the current stream; Tensor methods are module-level bound functions; the dispatch table is keyed by numel instead of a (numel, align) tuple; launcher closures take only (tensor, address); the lookup, dtype/contiguity validation and the launcher call happen in one Python frame. Kernels, BLOCK selection, masked/strided paths and the profiler gate are unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: Nine of twelve timing workloads are host-launch bound (profiled device task 1.65 us against a 13.16 us walltime for selu_-timing-0), so removing per-call Python dispatch work, not device work, is what moves the headline metric; a target-side interleaved A/B measured the shipped form at 11.50 us versus 12.17 us for the current path.

expected_effect.mechanism: Host-side per-call work drops by the ~0.7 us measured on target (12.17 -> 11.50 us per call), and the nine host-bound timing workloads carry only 1.65 us of device task, so their walltime latency should fall almost one-for-one.

profile.summary: mixed: Small workloads: >=87% of eval walltime is outside the profiled device kernel, Large bf16: vector pipe is 2.08x the fp16 control at identical byte volume; the fp32 upcast branch is the mechanism, Large fp32: device task is 1.57x the reference-side device time and is vector-dominated, not transfer-dominated

conclusion.root_cause: Confirmed the round-1 root cause for the host-bound majority: with only 1.65 us of device task per call, the per-call Python dispatch and launcher arguments were the whole cost, and removing the tuple key, the per-call method lookups and the extra closure frame cut 0.3-1.8 us per call. The remaining host floor is the compiled Triton launcher itself (~9.2 us per call, versus ~5.5-7.2 us for the full torch reference op), which is not reducible from the wrapper, so those workloads now sit at roughly the achievable limit (0.87-0.92 except where reference drift dominates).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted a ~0.7 us per-call host saving on the nine host-bound workloads (measured 12.17 -> 11.50 us on target) and observed exactly that direction: timing-0 13.164 -> 12.848 us, timing-2 12.777 -> 12.410, timing-5 14.371 -> 12.543, timing-6 13.804 -> 12.531, timing-10 12.349 -> 12.440, while timing-8/9 moved the other way by 0.6-1.0 us (12.786 -> 13.387, 12.359 -> 13.324). Aggregate geo_mean rose 0.8252 -> 0.8839 (+7.1%), larger than the 5.5% host-path delta because the reference latencies for those workloads were also measured higher this round (timing-1 reference 10.712 -> 13.804 us, giving that workload 0.825 -> 1.090), so part of the aggregate gain is reference-side drift rather than candidate improvement. The three large workloads were unchanged by design (same kernels, BLOCK and grid): timing-3 45.588 -> 45.603 us (1.249 -> 1.248) and timing-7 83.246 -> 83.310 us (0.710) reproduce round 1, while timing-11 measured 82.649 -> 92.166 us (0.596 -> 0.572) even though its device path is byte-identical, and its reference moved 49.301 -> 52.681 us in the same direction, so that entry is device-level drift on a shared card, not a regression from this change; a target probe measured the same fp32 config at 83.8 and 98.4 us in two consecutive runs, bounding that noise at roughly +/-15%.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Attack the bf16 large case with the already-probed narrowing: bf16 currently runs fp32-domain math, which needs three full-width UB tiles and caps BLOCK at 8192 (2048 MTE transfers, 83.3 us); doing the math at fp16 width compiles at BLOCK 16384 (1024 transfers) and was probed at 64.45 us with 0 of 16777216 elements outside the bf16 tolerance, so expect selu_-timing-7 to move from 0.71 toward 0.9.
conclusion.debug_lesson: On the walltime-timed small workloads the reference latency itself moves 10-30% between rounds (timing-1 reference 10.71 us in round 1 vs 13.80 us in round 2), so a single round's per-workload speedup at the ~12 us scale is not by itself evidence about a code change; only changes large enough to clear that noise, or device-task-duration evidence, should drive the next experiment.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 established two separate regimes; round 2 spent the whole round on the host-launch regime because it covers nine of twelve timing workloads. That lever is now largely exhausted, so the next round moves to the device regime for bf16 (transfer count via tile width), and fp32 remains the open problem because no BLOCK 16384 form compiles for fp32-domain math.

plan.strategy: Narrow the bf16 math width so the bf16 tile can double, halving its MTE transfer count.
plan.code_changes: _selu_nomask/_selu_masked gain an explicit bfloat16 branch that casts the loaded tile to float16, runs the same fp16-width expression, and rounds the result back to bfloat16; _pick_block now caps BLOCK at 8192 only for float32 (16384 for fp16 and bf16). fp32 path, strided kernel, host dispatch and profiler gate unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: bf16 runs fp32-domain math, whose three live full-width UB tiles cap BLOCK at 8192 and therefore double the MTE transfer count; doing the math at fp16 width fits BLOCK 16384. Target probe at n=16777216: 83.82 us for the current bf16 form versus 64.45 us for the fp16-width form, with 0 of 16777216 elements outside the bf16 tolerance (max abs error 0.0175).

expected_effect.mechanism: Halving the bf16 program count halves the MTE transfers (2048 -> 1024 for 16.7M elements), which is the cost driver measured on this target.

conclusion.root_cause: The bf16 root cause is confirmed and was fixed as predicted: bf16 was running fp32-domain math, which needs three live full-width UB tiles and therefore caps BLOCK at 8192, doubling the MTE transfer count relative to fp16 at BLOCK 16384; the fp16-width bf16 branch compiles at 16384 and delivers the predicted 63.5 us. The aggregate regression has a different, unrelated cause: bilateral machine-level drift of about 12% on the host-bound small workloads between the round-2 and round-3 measurements, which the retest quantified and which no code change in this round could have produced.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: The frozen expectation was that halving the bf16 transfer count would move selu_-timing-7 from 0.71 toward 0.90, and the workload-level evidence matched exactly: 83.310 -> 63.477 us, speedup 0.710 -> 0.932, versus the 64.45 us that the pre-round target probe predicted, with correctness unchanged (0 bad elements; bf16 correctness cases still 1.0 matched ratio, max rel err 0.044). The aggregate nevertheless fell from 0.8839 to 0.8670 because the nine small workloads, whose kernels and host path are byte-identical to round 2 and which this change cannot affect, all moved +1.5 to +2.0 us together with their own reference latencies. A full-suite retest confirmed the drift was bilateral and not the candidate: reference latencies returned to 10.46-11.75 us (from 11.94-13.30) and candidate latencies to 11.64-13.66 us, giving a remeasured geo_mean of 0.8727 with timing-7 (63.472 us) and timing-11 (82.682 us) unchanged within 0.1%. So the device change delivered its predicted 31% on timing-7, while the headline metric moved the opposite way purely through measurement drift on the host-bound majority; the round is not an improvement on the ledger even though its kernel is strictly better on the one workload it targets.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Re-establish the verified bf16 narrowing (it is a real 83.3 -> 63.5 us device win on selu_-timing-7 and has no effect on any other dtype, since the bf16 branch is compile-time eliminated elsewhere) and, in the same submission, recover the remaining host-side slack measured on target by dropping the extra Python frame and the unused tensor argument on the launcher call, then verify the combined form under the retest path if the two sides drift again.
conclusion.debug_lesson: A geo_mean comparison across rounds on this shared card is only meaningful if both sides moved together: here the reference latencies for the nine small workloads swung 11.7 -> 12.5 -> 11.2 us mean across three measurements of the same code, which is larger than any host-path change made so far. Round-to-round comparisons therefore need the retest path or a per-workload device-task measurement before concluding that a candidate regressed.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 2 exhausted the host-launch lever; round 3 moved to the device/transfer-count regime and its mechanism was verified per workload, but the ledger decision is dominated by drift on the other twelve-twelfths of the suite. Strategy changes accordingly: subsequent rounds must pair a verified device win with same-state verification (retest) rather than trusting a single cross-round aggregate.
